catalog_quote: [Rialland & Robert 2001: 899-900] The second point of note is that there is no melodic marking of accents. Higher pitch (or even lower pitch, as would appear in a language like Danish) is nowhere used to mark accent. Wolof is nevertheless typologically a language with stress.13 The basic stress-placement rule is as follows: stress falls on the first syllable of lexemes unless the second syllable is long, in which case it falls on the latter (Sauvageot 1965: 41–44; Njie 1982: 53; Ka 1988: 219–242, 1994). The two short examples (7a) and (7b), each of which contains two stresses (one on the subject Peer and the other on the verb lekk),14 already suffice to show that pitch height is not linked to stress. ... sweep_summary: Wolof (nucl1347), catalog classification weight on Rialland & Robert 2001 (citing Ka 1988). Five title hits: three are Glottolog machine misassignments (Lucci 1983 and Di Cristo 2016 on French via the word 'contemporain'; Jackson & Lewis 2005 CUNY poster via 'operator') — none are Wolof sources, priority none. Cissé 2009 (Sciences et techniques du langage 6, Dakar) is a genuine Wolof item but about prosodic phrasing for oral-expression teaching; no online copy exists (Crossref, HAL, archive.org, Bing all empty), print-only, low priority. Ka 1990 was obtained open from the archive.org scan of SLS vol. 20 (saved with the extracted article, scanned text and page scan under, ledgered): p. 113 characterizes the Wolof foot as binary, left-dominant following Ka 1988's stress analysis, p. 119 calls this 'the Wolof stress algorithm' — consistent with initial stress, silent on the weight clause, does not supersede the catalog source. The catalog's classification stands; Robert 2011 (downloaded in the earlier reading) independently states the same first-syllable-unless-second-is-long rule. Best acquisition target for a primary statement remains Ka 1988 (Wolof phonology and morphology: a nonlinear approach, UIUC PhD), which both the catalog source and Ka 1990 rely on; it was not among the works with stress in the title and was not sought here.

new_statements.reading: Wolof feet are binary and left-headed (strong-weak), i.e. prominence on the first syllable of the foot, per the author's own 1988 stress analysis. This supports the catalog's initial-stress clause but does not state the long-second-syllable (weight) condition; it is a second-hand pointer to Ka 1988 rather than a full stress rule. Robert 2011 (already held by the project, p. 4 §D: 'l'accent principal porte sur la première syllabe d'un terme, sauf si la deuxième est longue') gives the full rule and matches the catalog's 'weight' coding.

sources.citation: Bell, Arthur J. 2003. Gemination, degemination and moraic structure in Wolof. Working Papers of the Cornell Phonetics Laboratory 15: 1-68. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3731718
sources.quote: 'The canonical position for primary stress is the leftmost syllable of the word ... Primary stress appears on the second syllable only when that syllable contains a long vowel and the first syllable does not' (ko.máa.se, xan.dóor, deg.góo); 'all syllables with short vowels are light, including open syllables; syllables closed by a consonant; and syllables closed by a geminate'; syllables closed by a glide also light (sEy.lÉEn); 'heavy syllables are unique in attracting secondary stress' (wax.táa.nu.kàay, xáa.raa.nàat) and 'two adjacent syllables cannot both be stressed'.
sources.note: downloaded now; supplies the secondary-stress statement our the secondary-stress rule says is unstated (secondary stress on non-initial long-vowel syllables, no clash) and explicit light status of CVC, geminate-closed and glide-closed syllables.

sources.citation: Jacobs, Haike. 2022. Moras are about length not about weight: Cayuga laryngeal metathesis, Chugach Alutiiq degemination and Wolof stress. Linguistics in the Netherlands 39: 104-121. doi:10.1075/avt.00064.jac
sources.quote: Secondary theoretical treatment (data from Ka 1988, Bell 2003): 'Stress is on the first syllable ... If the first syllable contains a short vowel and the second syllable a long vowel, stress is on the second syllable'; 'A coda consonant does not make a syllable heavy' ([ˈpɛ.tax]); geminate-closed first syllable skipped ([degːˈoː]); analysed as a quantity-sensitive initial trochee with WSP-vowel.
sources.note: The abstract states that Wolof stress treats syllables with long vowels as heavy but syllables closed by a geminate as light, even though both are bimoraic. This adds the weight criterion (vowel length only) to the catalog's bare weight entry; the paper is a theoretical argument (Harmonic Serialism) with no measurements.
sources.venue: Linguistics in the Netherlands

sources.note: The work contains no statement about word stress, accent placement or tone in Wolof. The only prosody-adjacent material is orthographic: a short/long a distinction (long a written with a circumflex) and two accented e's (é, è), plus remarks that nasal vowels are absent or very rare and that final consonants are always pronounced. The 'accents' are diacritics for vowel quality/length, not stress marks. Vowel length is the basis of the catalog's weight criterion (heavy = long vowel), but the work does not connect length to stress, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog entry. Nothing
